name: Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)
autonymMeaning: the villages descended from the ancestor Banɔl
parler: Fɔ́mbɔ́ (close to Tunen); Basaa as a second language
overview: The Ndog-Banɔl, whom their neighbours call Fɔmbɔ, form a small group of 21 villages, bordering the Inoubou-Nord canton, the Alinga, the Basaa of Sanaga-Maritime, the Ndog-Biakat and the Yengui. Settled on a land of welcome, a former military camp, they live from cocoa, food crops and gathering.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group of 21 villages, both isolated and integrated with its neighbours (Inoubou-Nord, Alinga of Nitoukou, Basaa of Sanaga-Maritime, Ndog-Biakat, Yengui).
All also speak Basaa.
Marriages mostly within the group; men more often marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: It is not the ancestral land but a land of welcome, a former military camp.
The Ndog-Banɔl come from nine villages (Ndog Bekom, Ndog Tok Mbek, Ndog Basoni, Ndog Nyoki, Etou, Ndog Bikak…), with no surviving links.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Class, kinship and age structure society; the chief decides from above, but also by consensus.
Anyone can interact freely, including unmarried people and in-laws, as long as it does not cause a problem.
Of the nine original subgroups, only two can inherit from each other.
Relations with certain Basaa neighbours retain traces of historical grudges.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family.
The boy became a man when he could climb the palm tree for wine and bunches, then when he had his own house; the girl, by presenting her fiancé to her parents.
No fixed age, but young girls do not marry before 17.
Steps: meeting, courtesy visit, inquiry into morals, request, engagement, bride price. Palm wine and cola express acceptance and consent.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cult of the nənəm: people went there when needed, no more than once a year, to fight an epidemic or famine, or to ask for the prosperity of the village.
The nənəm, a cave or hill, and a lake where the initiated fished for medicinal water lilies are found at Ndog-Nyɔk.
Birth is the return of a forebear; death, the return to the ancestors, protectors and counsellors.
Incest taboo. The woman never inherits the throne and eats neither doe (sɔ́), nor monitor lizard, nor tortoise, nor civet; the man must not damage the part of the palm tree that yields wine.
Killing exposes one to mbàk, a serious defilement; desecrating graves is forbidden.
Divination: the ngǎm, a form of clairvoyance.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, cocoa, gathering. Women: groundnut, cocoyam, cassava.
The land belongs to the men: paternal inheritance or customary transfer.
Ancestral crafts: carrying baskets and baskets.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly loincloth; then wrapper and shirt for men, kaba and skirt for women.
Traditional medicine remains widely used.
Beauty: the robust, tall, strong man; the dark-skinned, full-figured, well-built woman.
Courtship: dancer, wrestler, hunter; the woman a good singer, hard-working and maternal.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: òbɔ̀k, ǹkūsé, ǹkolbitsé, nə̀hás, on the tam-tam and the drum; bɔ̀k dance.
No community festival of its own.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Food, clothing and crafts bring the Ndog-Banɔl closer to the Ndog-Ban.

sections.title: The names
items: Most men's names begin with ba-, women's with kū-; twin boys: Esɔ̀mɔ́ (small) and Elumú (big); twin girls: Sén (elder) and Sòl (younger).
The name is consecrated on the 9th day at a rite; traditionally it is not changed.
Kinship terms: àwáyà (brother, cousin), ìlòk (uncle's wife), mòlá (uncle), anatata (brother's child).
The founder, Banɔ́l, bears a name that means “he was stripped”.

lessons.title: Who are the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Minority group of 21 villages, at once isolated and integrated with its neighbours (Inoubou-Nord, Alinga of Nitoukou, Basaa of Sanaga-Maritime, Ndog-Biakat, Yengui). • All also speak Basaa. • Marriages mostly within the group; men more often marry outside. • It is not the ancestral land but a land of welcome, a former military camp. • The Ndog-Banɔl come from nine villages (Ndog Bekom, Ndog Tok Mbek, Ndog Basoni, Ndog Nyoki, Etou, Ndog Bikak…), with no ties kept.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ndog-Banɔl, whom their neighbours call Fɔmbɔ, form a small group of 21 villages, bordering the Inoubou-Nord canton, the Alinga, the Basaa of Sanaga-Maritime, the Ndog-Biakat and the Yengui. Settled on a land of welcome, a former military camp, they live from cocoa, food crops and gathering.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: mets de pistache et bâtons de manioc

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: hìkɔ̀k with taro or cassava, pistachio dishes and cassava sticks, mbongo tʃɔ̀bi, koki, bushmeat. • Drinks: palm wine. • Men: farming, cocoa, gathering. Women: groundnuts, macabo, cassava.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) mainly eat hìkɔ̀k with taro or cassava, pistachio-seed dishes and cassava sticks, mbongo tʃɔ̀bi, koki. Traditional drinks: palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) woman. What steps will he have to follow?

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

Palm wine and kola nut express acceptance and consent.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: òbɔ̀k, ǹkūsé, ǹkolbitsé, nə̀hás, on the tam-tam and the drum; bɔ̀k dance. • No community festival of its own.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), traditional dances (bɔ̀k) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover the music and dances of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), then learn to perform one.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: List the dances and say on what occasion each one is performed.

activities.title: I describe
activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), traditional dances (bɔ̀k) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, cocoa, gathering. Women: groundnuts, cocoyam, cassava. • Land belongs to men: paternal inheritance or customary transfer. • Ancestral crafts: carrying baskets and baskets.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, cocoa, gathering. Women: groundnut, cocoyam, cassava. Land belongs to men: paternal inheritance or customary transfer.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, cocoa, gathering. Women: groundnut, cocoyam, cassava. Land belongs to men: paternal inheritance or customary transfer.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: biche, varan, tortue, civette pour les femmes

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the nənəm: people went there when needed, no more than once a year, to fight an epidemic or famine, or to ask for the village's prosperity. • The nənəm, a cave or hill, and a lake where initiates fished for medicinal water lilies are found at Ndog-Nyɔk. • Birth is the return of an ancestor; death, the return to the ancestors, protectors and advisers. • Taboo of incest. A woman never inherits the throne and eats neither doe (sɔ́), nor monitor lizard, nor tortoise, nor civet; a man must not damage the part of the palm tree that gives wine. • Killing exposes one to mbàk, a serious defilement; desecrating graves is forbidden.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cult of the nənəm: people went there when needed, no more than once a year, to fight an epidemic or famine, or to ask for the prosperity of the village. The nənəm, a cave or hill, and a lake where initiates fished for medicinal water lilies are found at Ndog-Nyɔk.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Cult of the nənəm: people went there when needed, no more than once a year, to fight an epidemic or famine, or to ask for the prosperity of the village. The nənəm, a cave or hill, and a lake where initiates fished for medicinal water lilies are found at Ndog-Nyɔk.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Fɔ́mbɔ́
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Fɔ́mbɔ́. • Greeting formulae: òpàgà = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Ònájá/wàjá = morning greeting (one person); nùàjáé = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bómɔ́tɛ́, Béfándɛ̀, bèlàl, Bí nûs, Bè láh. • The founder, Banɔ́l, bears a name meaning “he was stripped”. • Cooking, clothing and crafts bring the Ndog-Banɔl close to the Ndog-Ban.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Fɔ́mbɔ́ are the first steps towards communicating with the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Fɔ́mbɔ́.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Fɔ́mbɔ́ are the first steps towards communicating with the Fɔ́mbɔ́ (Ndog-Banɔl). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
